Subject: Data lifecycle controls: retention caps & field tokenization options for MedAxis

Hi Rishi,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — team was impressed with the latency numbers. We need to lock down the data lifecycle side for PHI/PII before we start ingesting production notes. High level asks:

- Retention caps: MedAxis policy requires free-text clinical notes removed within 180 days; structured metadata (visit timestamps, encounter ids) retained up to 3 years for audit.
- De-identification: we need an option for reversible pseudonymization (only reversible under court order / on legal hold) but would also like an irreversible hash option for lower-risk fields.
- Search/analytics implications: can you summarize how each approach (tokenization, hashing, truncation, full deletion) affects our ability to do semantic search and embeddings, and what the cost/latency tradeoffs are?
- Evidence: we will need SOC2-relevant artifacts and a short summary of how logs/audit trails and KMS usage are captured.

Attached a simple spreadsheet with expected daily volume (rows/day) and example fields. Can you review and propose options?

Also looped procurement (procurement@medaxis.com) for the commercial ask.

Thanks,

Subject: Re: Data lifecycle controls: retention caps & field tokenization options for MedAxis

Alex — thanks for the clear brief and the volume sheet. Quick summary of practical options from a Redwood operational perspective (high level):

1) Tenant TTL + automated deletion (recommended when you can tolerate data loss after X days)
   - Implementation: per-tenant TTL on stored objects + background job to remove KV cache and embeddings.
   - Pros: lowest long-term storage cost, simplest audit trail (deletion events).
   - Cons: irrevocable; search/analytics over deleted text not possible.

2) Field-level reversible tokenization (pseudonymization)
   - Implementation: tokenize PHI fields before persistent storage; token map encrypted with your KMS (HSM-backed option). Reversal requires both Redwood + customer KMS key access and a legal-hold workflow.
   - Pros: preserves ability to rehydrate for clinical workflows, allows embeddings to be built on de-identified text if you replace tokens consistently.
   - Cons: slightly higher latency on ingest and cost for encrypted token vaults; requires strict key management & audit.

3) Irreversible hashing with salt
   - Implementation: salted hash on identifiers; store only hash for dedup/lookup.
   - Pros: strong privacy guarantees; cheap and fast.
   - Cons: cannot re-associate; limits usefulness for record reconciliation that requires identity recovery.

4) Redaction or truncation at ingest (remove or truncate identified spans)
   - Implementation: remove PHI spans using regex/NLP on ingest and index the redacted text.
   - Pros: minimal compliance surface, predictable cost.
   - Cons: degraded model outputs / embeddings; harder to match across records.

Search & embeddings notes: if you strip or redact before embedding, embeddings will reflect the redacted view (semantic loss). A common compromise: build embeddings on de-identified text where named entities are replaced with stable tokens (e.g., [PATIENT_123]) — preserves contextual meaning while removing raw PHI.

I attached a simple diagram that maps these approaches to cost and operational controls.

Next steps I need from you: confirmation whether MedAxis needs reversible mapping for day-to-day clinical lookups (yes/no), and whether legal-hold reversibility should be tightly gated to an approval workflow. Also helpful: expected 95th percentile doc length — that drives batching and KV sizing.

If you prefer, we can do a 30-minute call tomorrow to walk the options and map to your SOC2 scope.

Best,
Rishi Malhotra
Enterprise Solutions
Redwood Inference

Alex / Rishi — adding Compliance perspective and a few guardrails we typically require for regulated PHI workflows. Short bullets to make this actionable: 

- Legal hold override: implement a legal-hold flag stored in a tamper-evident audit trail (append-only) that prevents TTL deletion and records who placed the hold and why. Reversal of tokenization requires multi-party approval (Redwood SRE + MedAxis legal) and a documented request (we can pipeline this into our ticketing & audit system).

- KMS & key custody: for reversible tokenization we require customer-managed KMS keys (preferred) or Redwood-managed HSM-backed keys with strict role separation. Key usage events must be logged and retained for the SOC2 period (we typically keep key usage logs for 3 years).

- Backups & snapshots: snapshots of storage are retained per our backup policy; we can support shorter snapshot retention for your tenant (e.g., 30/90/365 days) but note that snapshots are a common source of retained PHI — we will configure snapshot pruning aligned to your retention choice.

- Embeddings & analytics: to preserve utility while minimizing PHI exposure we recommend deterministic tokenization of named entities (stable mapping) and hashing of identifiers that are not needed for re-identification. This allows cross-document semantic search via embeddings while keeping raw PHI out of indexable text.

- SOC2 evidence and mapping: we will provide an artifact bundle showing configuration (retention TTL settings), key rotation policy, KMS access logs, deletion job run logs, and the legal-hold audit. We can redact specific internal hostnames from the bundle for vendor sharing.

Suggested operational baseline for MedAxis (proposal):
  - Free-text clinical notes: 180-day TTL (auto-delete), reversible pseudonymization as an optional add-on (with customer KMS) with legal-hold override.
  - Structured metadata: 3-year retention, hashed patient identifiers for analytics unless explicit reversible mapping is requested.
  - Backups: 90-day snapshot retention by default (extendable).
  - Logs/audit: 3-year retention aligned with SOC2 evidence requirements.

Costs/impacts: reversible token vault adds ~5–12% to storage/ops cost depending on volume and rotation frequency; embedding rebuilds after a rehydration event are billable as batch compute.

I can assemble the SOC2 artifact checklist and a short mutual action plan if you want to proceed.

Regards,
Monica Patel
Sr. Compliance Manager
Redwood Inference
